title: Word filtration for a free simplicial-category arrow attachment
statement:
Use small simplicial categories, simplicial sets and the two-object simplicial category $U(K)$ of [lem-coef-simplicial-interval-lifting]. Let $K\hookrightarrow L$ be a degreewise injective map of small simplicial sets, let $C$ be a small simplicial category, and let $h:U(K)\to C$ be an enriched functor selecting objects $x,y$ (possibly equal) and a simplicial map $K\to C(x,y)$. Form $C^+=C\amalg_{U(K)}U(L)$ in the category of simplicial categories with arbitrary object functions.

The objects of $C^+$ are the objects of $C$. For $w,z\in C$, put $M_0=C(w,z)$ and, for $k\geq1$, put
$$H_k=C(y,z)\times C(y,x)^{k-1}\times C(w,x),\qquad M_k=H_k\times L^k.$$
The factors are ordered as alternating words $(a_0,t_1,a_1,\ldots,t_k,a_k)$ from $w$ to $z$, with $a_0:y\to z$, $a_k:w\to x$, and the intermediate $a_i:y\to x$. There is a natural isomorphism from $C^+(w,z)$ to the quotient of $\coprod_{k\geq0}M_k$ by the relations replacing any $t_j\in K$ by $h(t_j)$ and composing the two adjacent $C$-arrows with it; composition concatenates words and composes the two adjacent old arrows.

Let $P_k$ be the image of words of length at most $k$ in this quotient. Then $P_0=C(w,z)$, each $P_{k-1}\to P_k$ is a monomorphism, and $C^+(w,z)=\operatorname{colim}_{k\geq0}P_k$. For $k\geq1$, let $Q_k\subseteq L^k$ be the simplicial subset consisting degreewise of tuples having at least one coordinate in $K$, and put $N_k=H_k\times Q_k\subseteq M_k$. The square with top map $N_k\hookrightarrow M_k$, left map $N_k\to P_{k-1}$ given by the stated reduction relations, and bottom map $P_{k-1}\to P_k$ is a pushout of simplicial sets. These presentations and squares are natural under every simplicial functor $F:C\to D$, using the attaching map $Fh$ on $D$, even when $F$ identifies objects. In particular $C\to C^+$ is identity on objects and a monomorphism on every mapping simplicial set. Pushouts and colimits have the universal-property meaning of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit].

source.place: Proposition A.3.2.4, proof, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877): explicit words, reduction relations, and the filtration by their length. No Stacks tag states this enriched-category construction. Read online; archival copy WANTED.

proof.text: Identify $K_n$ with its image in $L_n$ for each degree $n$; injectivity makes the preimage used by $h$ unique. For fixed endpoints define $W_n=\coprod_{k\geq0}(M_k)_n$. Define $r(u,v)$ when $v$ is obtained by deleting one $t_j\in K_n$ and replacing the adjacent block by $a_{j-1}\circ h(t_j)\circ a_j$. This has the required endpoints, also when $x=y$. Let $E(w,z)_n=W_n/{\sim}$, where $\sim$ is the equivalence relation generated by $r$. Apply a simplicial operator to every coordinate of a representative word. It takes a reduction to a reduction, since $K$ is a simplicial subset and $h$ and composition are simplicial maps. Thus the coordinatewise operators descend to $E(w,z)$, and their identities follow on every representative from the identities on $C$ and $L$. This directly constructs the simplicial quotient without invoking a theorem that colimits commute with evaluation.

proof.text: Check the strong diamond condition for $r$ in a fixed degree. Two reductions in the same coordinate give the same word; take that word as the common target. Two reductions at distinct nonadjacent coordinates commute, since they change disjoint blocks. For adjacent coordinates, the two possible double reductions both replace the five-arrow block by $a_{j-1}\circ h(t_j)\circ a_j\circ h(t_{j+1})\circ a_{j+1}$, with equality by associativity in $C$. The other marked $K_n$-coordinate remains present after the first deletion, so both second reductions exist. Hence in the distinct-coordinate case each first reduct reaches the same word by one further step. These are precisely the hypotheses of the common-reduct lemma, with equality or one step on its first side and zero or more on the second.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-rewrite-common-reduct] degreewise. Its relation $J$ is an equivalence relation containing $r$ (for $r(u,v)$ use the common target $v$). Conversely any common reduct supplies a zigzag of reductions, so $J$ is contained in $\sim$. Since $\sim$ is the least equivalence relation containing $r$, it equals $J$. Every word reaches an irreducible word: induct on its length, stopping if no coordinate is in $K_n$, otherwise deleting one such coordinate and using the induction hypothesis at length one less. Two irreducible representatives of the same class have a common reduct by $J$, and a reduction path starting at an irreducible word is constant. They are therefore equal as words, including all old-arrow labels. It follows that classes are in bijection with words whose $L_n$-coordinates all lie outside $K_n$. This is only a degreewise description; simplicial operators can take such coordinates into $K$, so no simplicial complement of $K$ is asserted.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Give $E$ object set $\operatorname{Ob}C$ and compose words by concatenating them and composing the two old arrows at the join. A reduction away from the join is still the same reduction in the concatenation. At the join of positive-length words $u=(a_0,t_1,\ldots,t_k,a_k)$ and $v=(b_0,s_1,\ldots,s_l,b_l)$, reducing $t_k\in K$ before or after joining gives $(a_{k-1}\circ h(t_k)\circ a_k)\circ b_0=a_{k-1}\circ h(t_k)\circ(a_k\circ b_0)$. Reducing $s_1\in K$ gives $(a_k\circ b_0)\circ h(s_1)\circ b_1=a_k\circ(b_0\circ h(s_1)\circ b_1)$. If either word has length zero, the same equalities omit the absent new coordinate. Thus each join case is associativity in $C$. Thus changing either representative by a generating relation leaves the composite class unchanged, and composition descends. For three words, both parenthesizations have the same new coordinates; their old coordinates coincide by associativity in $C$, including when a word has length zero. The identity at $w$ is the length-zero word $1_w$, and both unit laws follow from those of $C$. Coordinatewise simplicial operators preserve these compositions and identities. Thus $E$ is a small simplicial category. The length-zero words define a functor $C\to E$; the word $(1_y,t,1_x)$ defines a simplicial map $L\to E(x,y)$ whose restriction to $K$ equals $h$ by a single reduction.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Verify the enriched pushout universal property. A cocone to a small simplicial category $B$ consists of a functor $G:C\to B$ and a map $\ell:L\to B(Gx,Gy)$ restricting to $Gh$ on $K$; this is exactly the data of a functor $U(L)\to B$ agreeing on $U(K)$, even if its two objects have the same image. Evaluate a word by $G(a_0)\circ\ell(t_1)\circ G(a_1)\circ\cdots\circ\ell(t_k)\circ G(a_k)$. Reduction leaves this value unchanged because $\ell|_K=Gh$ and $G$ preserves composition. Evaluation is simplicial, preserves concatenation and identities, and gives a functor $E\to B$. Every word is the composite of its old arrows and the words $(1_y,t_j,1_x)$, so any extending functor must have this value; its object function is already fixed by $G$. This proves existence and uniqueness of the extension. Hence $E$ is the specified pushout $C^+$ by the universal-property definition, with the asserted quotient and composition.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Let $P_k$ be the image of all words of length at most $k$ in $E(w,z)$. Applying a simplicial operator does not increase the length of a representative, so these images are simplicial subsets and their inclusions are monomorphisms: two maps followed by a subset inclusion agree only if their values already agree. By the unique irreducible description from step 3, the length-zero words are pairwise distinct; thus $P_0$ identifies with $C(w,z)$ as a simplicial set. In degree $n$, $P_k$ consists exactly of classes with irreducible length at most $k$, because reductions strictly decrease length. For $k\geq1$, the subset $N_k\subset M_k$ consists of words with some coordinate in $K$. A simplicial operator keeps that coordinate in $K$ and acts coordinatewise on $H_k$, so $Q_k$ and $N_k$ are simplicial subsets. Every such word has a first reduction of length $k-1$, so its image in $E(w,z)$ lies in $P_{k-1}$. Restricting the quotient map therefore gives a simplicial map $N_k\to P_{k-1}$. It equals the class of any of the stated first reductions, because each is equivalent to the original word. This proves the required independence when several coordinates are in $K$, and commutation with every simplicial operator.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Prove the attachment square by its universal property. In each degree, a class in $P_k$ either belongs to $P_{k-1}$ or has a unique irreducible word of length exactly $k$. A word in $(M_k)_n\setminus(N_k)_n$ is irreducible, represents a new class, and no two such words represent the same class. Every word in $(N_k)_n$ represents the old class prescribed by the left map. Given simplicial maps $u:P_{k-1}\to T$ and $v:M_k\to T$ agreeing on $N_k$, define the value on an old class by $u$ and on a new class by $v$ of its unique length-$k$ word. For an arbitrary representative in $M_k$, this value is $v$: on $N_k$ it follows from the agreement, and off $N_k$ from uniqueness. Thus after any simplicial operator it is still computed by $u$ or $v$ on the operated representative, and their simpliciality proves the defined map $P_k\to T$ is simplicial, even when a new class becomes old. These representatives cover $P_k$, proving uniqueness. This is exactly the pushout universal property, and gives the square with the claimed maps.

source.place: HTT, proof of Proposition A.3.2.4, printed pp.859-860 (PDF pp.876-877); agent supplies the omitted checks.

proof.text: Every word is finite, so $E(w,z)=\bigcup_{k\geq0}P_k$. A compatible family of simplicial maps $P_k\to T$ defines a map on this union by evaluating a class in any stage containing it; two choices agree in the larger stage. The resulting map is simplicial since each $P_k$ is a simplicial subset, and it is unique. This proves the stated sequential colimit. For any enriched functor $F:C\to D$, send a word to the word with old labels $F(a_i)$ and unchanged new labels $t_j$, and endpoints $Fw,Fz$. A generating reduction maps to the same reduction because $F(a\circ h(t)\circ b)=F(a)\circ(Fh)(t)\circ F(b)$. These maps therefore descend to the quotients, preserve length bounds and carry $N_k$ to the corresponding $N_k$ for $D$. They commute with each quotient map and reduction map, hence with every map in the squares and the colimit cocones. Identity and composition of functors act identically and compositely on these labels. No step uses injectivity of the object function of $F$, so the naturality includes object identifications. Finally $C\to C^+$ is identity on objects by construction and mappingwise monic by the identification with $P_0$.
